newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambia presses on with poll, ignoring Mandela.
newsitem.headline: Zambia presses on with poll, ignoring Mandela.

text.p: Zambia's ruling party has rejected a call by South African President Nelson Mandela to postpone next week's elections and accused him of treating them like children.

"Mandela has no right to tell us to postpone an election," said Vernon Mwaanga, campaign chairman of President Frederick Chiluba's Movement for Multi-party Democracy (MMD), which is set to win the poll.
"We cannot be given instructions like schoolchildren."
Chiluba's office said that Mwaanga's remarks, made at a news conference late on Thursday, reflected the president's view.
Mandela, making an unprecedented public intervention over the disputed poll, urged Chiluba on Thursday to call it off in the face of mounting accusations it would be a sham.

Chiluba's rival and veteran predecessor, Kenneth Kaunda, has been barred from standing and his United National Independence Party (UNIP), the main opposition, is boycotting the poll in which voter cards have only reached a quarter of the 4.6 millon-strong electorate.

Rioting students in the capital Lusaka joined calls on Chiluba to reopen political dialogue with his opponents. Kaunda has called for a campaign of civil disobedience but pledged it would be peaceful.

After quiet diplomacy failed, including private talks with Chiluba in Pretoria on Tuesday, Mandela told a news conference he had faxed Chiluba urging the presidential and parliamentary vote be put off.
Pretoria's acting High Commissioner in Lusaka, Willem Swanepoel, said no reply had been received.

UNIP and six other opposition parties have mounted the boycott, saying the elections have been arranged to ensure Chiluba and his party secure another term of office after winning Zambia's first free elections in 1991 that put an end to three decades of one-party rule under Kaunda.

Their main complaint, as well as voter registration irregularities, is over a new constitution passed in May by Chiluba supporters that bars Kaunda and other opposition figures from standing for president.
The new law ruled Kaunda out because his parents, from Malawi, were not Zambian-born and because he had ruled for more than two terms.
A last-minute bid to stop the vote by opposition parties who said Chiluba had lied about his own parents' background failed on Thursday.

Political analysts say the MMD's manoeuvring has seriously damaged the popularity of a party and president who would have won anyway had they let Kaunda stand. Bad as life may be for ordinary Zambians, most still remember far harder times under Kaunda, diplomats said.
Kaunda led Zambia to independence from Britain and ruled until he gave in to pressure for free elections.

When it peacefully shook off Kaunda's one-party rule, secret police control and economic mismanagement, the new Zambia was hailed as a beacon of hope for Africa, especially the south where Mozambique and Angola still suffered civil war and South Africa was under white rule.

The World Bank says its privatisation campaign has been the best in Africa but foreign aid donors and Zambia's neighbours have looked on with dismay as hopes that a strong democracy will take root have faded.
Donors have frozen aid to relieve Zambia's massive foreign debt in protest at the rising political tensions.
The government blames criticism on friends of Kaunda, one of Africa's elder statesmen whose links with Mandela were very close during South Africa's anti-apartheid struggle.
"Kaunda's banning is not the real point," Pretoria's Swanepoel said. "It is the whole slide from democratic principles, and this started about two years ago."
